moduleTitle: Human nature and the human condition

note.specFocus: Christian beliefs about what it means to be human, the nature of the soul, and whether human beings survive bodily death.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
1.2 Human Nature and the Human Condition
Christians generally believe human beings are more than physical bodies: each person has a soul, made in the image of God, which gives them lasting spiritual significance.
Body and soul
• Genesis 2:7 describes God breathing "the breath of life" into Adam, who then "became a living being" — many Christians take this to show that human life and identity are God-given, not purely biological.
• Imago Dei: being made in God's image is understood to include the capacity for reason, moral choice, creativity and relationship — qualities thought to distinguish humans from animals.
• Most Christians believe the soul survives physical death and will ultimately be reunited with a transformed, resurrected body (1 Corinthians 15), rather than existing forever as a separate spirit alone.
Human weakness
• Christians also recognise a darker side to human nature: Original Sin, traced to Adam and Eve's disobedience in Genesis 3, is held to have left all humans with an inclination towards selfishness and wrongdoing.
• This creates tension in Christian anthropology: humans are simultaneously described as made in God's image (dignified, valuable) and as fallen (flawed, sinful) — both ideas shape Christian ethics and the need for salvation through Christ.
Non-religious views
• Humanists reject the idea of an immortal soul, arguing personality, memory and consciousness arise entirely from brain activity, and that human dignity and morality do not require belief in God or an afterlife.
Exam link: questions often ask you to contrast "religious" and "non-religious" beliefs about human nature — keep the Christian soul/imago Dei view clearly separate from the humanist, brain-based view.

questions.examTip: Make two separate points and develop each one. Link the development directly to the question.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Most Christians believe that human beings are made in the image of God (imago Dei, Genesis 1:27) and are given an immortal soul which is distinct from the physical body and survives physical death.

2. St Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15 that believers will ultimately receive a transformed, resurrected body, so the soul's immortality is linked to the Christian hope of bodily resurrection rather than the soul alone drifting on forever.
questions.question: Choose one religion. Outline two beliefs about the immortality of the soul in this religion.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Christians generally teach that because human beings are made in the image of God, every person has a soul that is distinct from the body and that will continue to exist after physical death.

A second consideration is: Genesis 2:7 describes God breathing the breath of life into Adam, which many Christians interpret as showing that human life and spiritual identity come directly from God and are not merely material.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Humanists and other non-religious thinkers argue that there is no scientific evidence for a soul separate from the brain; consciousness, personality and memory can all be explained as products of brain activity that end at death.

A further consideration is: Some within Christianity itself, such as Christian physicalists, argue the Bible's emphasis on bodily resurrection (rather than a separate immortal soul) suggests the whole person, not a detachable soul, is what God values and recreates.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: the strength of someone's view often depends on whether they trust religious testimony and revelation, or require scientific/empirical evidence before accepting a claim about life beyond the body. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.examTip: Use accurate Christian teaching, explain why each point matters, and in an evaluation compare arguments before reaching a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of imago Dei, body-soul teaching, resurrection and non-religious materialist views and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
